purpose: Backend-neutral test designs; not implemented or executed conformance tests.
profile_tag_semantics: Informational applicability labels, not automatic AND/OR test selection. Review explicit case IDs and variants for every claimed composition.

cases.title: Capability negotiation rejects unsupported reliability before publication
given: Adapters advertise supported channel contracts and deployment failure models; fixtures include Core NATS only and a durable broker.
Compile the same graph separately with live_latest, reliable_work, durable_control, and replay_archive requests.
fault_schedule: Disable each requested mandatory capability in turn: retained backlog, recoverable delivery, durable control, independent archive, or durable payload references.
Attempt validation, provisioning, and producer start through the normal public entrypoint.
assertions: A missing mandatory capability produces a typed incompatibility including the channel and missing guarantee before any producer starts.
Core-only cannot silently downgrade reliable_work/control/archive to best effort; an explicitly composed durable service is evaluated as part of the complete backend.
Supported live_latest is accepted only when its explicitly requested freshness/key semantics are implemented, even if the underlying broker has no native latest-value primitive.
evidence: Capability manifest and per-channel validation report identifying each requested guarantee, supported guarantee, and typed rejection.
Provision/start/publish side-effect trace showing no producer start or publication before an incompatible request is rejected.
cases.acceptance: Every unsupported profile is an expected rejection test that passes by rejecting; never mark it skipped or silently run weaker assertions. Zero publish or allocation side effects before rejection.
historical_evidence: New abstraction acceptance test derived from flow-type/consumer-override mismatch; no existing portable backend API.

cases.title: Reliable alerts survive concurrent newer publications in a live graph
given: A producer feeds a reliable alert subscriber and a live display subscriber; buffer capacity for the display is one.
Reliable subscriber is provisioned before producer start; alert IDs A and B are distinct.
fault_schedule: Publish A and fetch it at the reliable subscriber without settlement.
Request retry of A, then publish B before the retry becomes eligible.
Reconnect the reliable subscriber and complete both inputs.
assertions: A remains recoverable despite B and despite display drops.
Both A and B have a terminal accounted outcome; for this successful fixture both complete.
The compiler either separates incompatible retention classes or implements retention satisfying all accepted subscriptions.
evidence: Publish receipts and reliable-subscription delivery/settlement ledger for IDs A and B with the NAK and concurrent B publication timestamps.
Effective channel retention/subscription configuration plus final logical outcome set for both reliable and live subscribers.
cases.acceptance: Observed successful ID set equals {A,B}; no accepted reliable ID disappears during latest-only traffic. Backend configurations that cannot satisfy the graph reject it before start.
historical_evidence: Executed prior probe: retry-enabled REALTIME consumer received alert-2 after alert-1 was overwritten; max_msgs=1.

cases.title: Latest-value behavior is bounded and scoped to the requested camera key
given: Two camera keys A and B request latest-per-key retention with one waiting frame per key, maximum age 200 ms, and an explicit in-flight allowance.
Producer timestamps and harness clock are controlled; subscriber processing can be paused.
fault_schedule: Pause processing; publish A1, B1, then A2 through A100 while leaving B unchanged.
Resume at a clock value when both A100 and B1 are within the requested age.
Advance clock past the age limit, then reconnect a slow subscriber with additional frames queued.
assertions: A traffic does not evict the sole waiting B value; accepted latest-per-key contract is not implemented by one global slot.
No expired queued frame reaches the processing callback after the age check; documented in-flight exceptions are separately measured.
All overwrites, expiration, and slow-consumer losses are observable and local waiting bytes remain bounded.
evidence: Timestamped per-camera publication and processing ledger including A1..A100, B1, frame ages, and the controlled clock schedule.
Queue count/byte high-water snapshots and per-ID overwrite, expiry, reconnect, and slow-consumer drop events.
cases.acceptance: At resume the eligible waiting set includes A100 and B1; after expiry no expired waiting payload is processed. Queue and drop counters reconcile with generated IDs.
historical_evidence: Source audit: one max_msgs limit per node, independent of camera key; Core NATS alone does not supply latest-per-key retention.

cases.title: Fan-out and competing workers preserve logical subscription boundaries
given: Producer P has two logical children X and Y; X has three interchangeable replicas and Y has two.
Reliable profile uses 100 unique inputs and enough retention/credits to avoid deliberate drops; live profile allows only explicitly reported drops.
fault_schedule: Start all subscribers behind a ready barrier and publish 100 IDs.
Kill one X replica after receiving an input and before completion, then replace it.
Drain remaining work and compare records by logical child and message ID.
assertions: Reliable: each ID has a completed outcome for X and for Y; retries may duplicate deliveries but cannot send X-only work to Y or lose the other child interest.
Within a child, successful duplicate effects are governed by the execution/idempotency contract rather than a false exactly-once transport claim.
Live: no cross-subscription leakage and every observed gap has an allowed loss classification.
evidence: Per-logical-child, per-replica delivery and completed-outcome ledger covering all 100 input IDs before and after worker replacement.
Effective subscription inventory and worker kill/restart barrier trace distinguishing fan-out children from competing replicas.
cases.acceptance: Reliable completion sets for X and Y both equal all 100 generated IDs after recovery; topology contains one logical work-sharing subscription per child, not one competing subscription shared by distinct children.
historical_evidence: Existing architecture intentionally creates one durable per child-parent edge shared by interchangeable replicas; retain this sound behavior.

cases.title: Provisioning failures prevent producers from publishing into absent interest
given: Required consumer has not been created; publication into absent interest can discard data.
Harness can deny create-consumer API calls while allowing create-stream and publish calls.
fault_schedule: Deny one required consumer creation using a real authorization error.
Run provision/start; also inject timeout and resource-limit errors in separate parameterizations.
Restore API access and retry the same run provisioning.
assertions: Each failed attempt reports not-ready and does not start producers.
An already-exists response is accepted only after inspecting and validating the actual subscription.
Successful retry verifies all required consumer interest before allowing producer start.
evidence: Injected authorization/timeout/resource-limit API failures, provision readiness transitions, and producer-start event trace.
Read-back stream/consumer inventory after successful retry and receipt/delivery records for inputs published before delayed worker startup.
cases.acceptance: Zero published application inputs during failed provisioning. After successful retry, publish-before-worker-start inputs remain available to the delayed worker.
historical_evidence: Source audit: _ensure_consumer catches every exception and logs only; Interest-retention loss follows absent consumer.

cases.title: Reconciliation detects incompatible existing broker configuration
given: An existing stream or consumer has the desired name but incorrect retention, subject filter, replica count, ACK policy, or credit.
fault_schedule: Create the conflicting resource externally.
Run normal idempotent provisioning while denying the requested update in one parameterization.
Read back actual broker configuration before producer start.
assertions: Provisioning never reports success based only on a name match or swallowed update error.
Immutable incompatibilities fail with an actionable mismatch; mutable fields converge and are verified.
Concurrent identical provisioning is harmless and does not relax the desired contract.
evidence: Externally seeded configuration, desired configuration, reconciliation API trace, and post-reconciliation effective configuration diff.
Provision result and producer-start gate evidence for denied updates, immutable mismatches, and concurrent identical provisioners.
cases.acceptance: Producer starts only when the read-back effective configuration satisfies every mandatory field. Each denied incompatible update fails validation.
historical_evidence: Source audit: _ensure_stream suppresses failed updates and _ensure_consumer suppresses arbitrary create errors.

cases.title: Offline reliable subscribers and worker replacement recover accepted inputs
given: Logical durable subscription is provisioned but no worker is online; recovery bound R is declared by the adapter test profile.
fault_schedule: Publish IDs 1..20 while the worker is offline.
Start the worker, hold ID 1 unsettled, and kill the worker.
Replace it with a fresh process and drain.
assertions: Every accepted ID remains recoverable until complete or explicitly terminal.
Replacement binds the same logical subscription rather than abandoning a process-specific durable.
Acknowledge one delivery and ensure recovery does not rely on the original process memory.
evidence: Accepted-publication ledger for IDs 1..20 and per-ID replacement-worker delivery/terminal-outcome history.
Worker lifecycle and subscription identity trace with kill-before-settlement barrier and measured recovery elapsed time.
cases.acceptance: All 20 accepted IDs complete within R after dependencies recover; no unaccounted accepted IDs. Core-only must reject this profile under MSG-001.
historical_evidence: Positive contract for the existing preprovisioned durable design; current tests cover only some transport paths.

cases.title: Worker-fatal failure remains recoverable at the broker delivery limit
given: Processing retry allowance is zero; broker fixture reproduces max delivery 1 unless the adapter deliberately separates its transport recovery budget.
Healthy replacement worker can process the same valid input.
fault_schedule: Deliver valid input A to worker 1 at its final broker delivery.
Inject worker-fatal exception or kill immediately before completion.
Run the recovery mechanism and start worker 2.
assertions: A receives another actionable delivery or an explicit durable recovery task; merely retaining A in broker storage is not recovery.
Transport/worker failure does not consume the poison-data budget or silently drop valid A.
Exhausted-delivery observability identifies the original input until it is resolved.
evidence: Input delivery counts, worker-fatal injection timestamp, broker exhausted-delivery status/advisories, and durable recovery task or redelivery record.
Healthy replacement worker completion record for A and measured recovery time after dependency restoration.
cases.acceptance: Within R after worker replacement, A successfully completes; a zero-pending counter without a completed or explicit terminal outcome fails.
historical_evidence: Executed MaxDeliver=1 probe: NAK produced no redelivery, one stored record, zero pending and zero ack-pending.

cases.title: DLQ outage at final delivery cannot strand an input
given: Poison input A is at its last allowed processing/broker attempt.
DLQ and input data use independently faultable publish paths.
fault_schedule: Make DLQ publication fail or become unavailable.
Fail A processing and attempt the terminal handoff.
Restart the worker while DLQ remains unavailable, then restore DLQ access.
assertions: Original input or durable handoff intent survives until terminal record and required payload pin are confirmed.
Recovery does not depend on a NAK that exceeds a finite broker delivery limit.
After recovery A has a durable dead-letter outcome and cannot disappear into zero pending with no explanation.
evidence: Input A attempt ledger, injected DLQ publish failures, worker crash barriers, and durable pending-handoff evidence during the outage.
Post-restoration DLQ logical-outcome record, payload pin confirmation where applicable, and original-input settlement history.
cases.acceptance: After DLQ restoration and within R, exactly one logical terminal outcome identifies A; duplicate physical DLQ publications are either deduplicated or coalesced by stable identity.
historical_evidence: Source audit and executed MaxDeliver probe establish the stranding path; a real DLQ outage at budget exhaustion was not previously run.

cases.title: Poison wire data has an explicit terminal disposition
given: Inputs include malformed envelope bytes, unsupported wire version, and a valid envelope whose payload access fails transiently.
fault_schedule: Publish each specimen followed by a valid sentinel.
Trigger decoding independently of payload retrieval.
Inspect settlement, terminal records, and processing of the sentinel.
assertions: Malformed or unsupported data receives a documented terminal outcome with provenance; reliable inputs do not vanish through an unrecorded TERM.
Transient payload failures are classified separately and remain retryable; PAY-002 covers their recovery.
One poison input does not block the valid sentinel indefinitely.
evidence: Raw specimen hashes/transport identities, parse versus payload-load error classifications, and durable terminal/drop records.
Sentinel delivery/completion timing and settlement trace proving transient GET failures were not terminally discarded.
cases.acceptance: Every malformed accepted reliable ID has a durable terminal record within the configured poison handling deadline, and sentinel completes; no transient infrastructure error is classified as malformed bytes.
historical_evidence: Source audit and executed transient-blob probe: catch-all decode handler TERMs any exception without DLQ.

cases.title: Superseded delivery handles cannot terminally discard the current delivery
given: One input is delivered as handle h1 and redelivered as h2 after its lease expires; h2 has not completed.
fault_schedule: Register h2 as the current delivery.
Invoke the abstraction operation that discards/replaces local h1; separately attempt terminal settlement using stale h1.
Kill the worker holding h2 before completion and start a replacement.
assertions: Local supersession performs no terminal settlement of the logical broker message.
Stale destructive settlement is rejected or fenced by ownership/delivery generation.
The replacement can recover the input and its payload.
evidence: h1/h2 delivery-generation trace, local supersession events, attempted stale settlement, and actual broker settlement command log.
Replacement-worker redelivery/completion record with payload checksum after h2 worker death.
cases.acceptance: Input completes at the replacement within R; settlement history contains no TERM emitted as a side effect of local handle replacement.
historical_evidence: Executed broker probe: TERM of h1 after delivery h2 deleted the Interest-retained message and prevented future recovery.

cases.title: Status distinguishes empty, unavailable, and stranded work
given: Status API exposes pending, in-flight, terminal-unresolved/exhausted, and availability state rather than one overloaded integer.
fault_schedule: Create a final-delivery exhausted input that remains retained.
Read status, then deny broker management API or inject a timeout.
Restore access and resolve the exhausted input.
assertions: The exhausted record is not reported as all-work-completed merely because both ordinary pending counters are zero.
API failure returns unavailable/unknown and cannot be converted to empty.
Recovery and completion consumers can distinguish safe zero from unobservable state.
evidence: Status responses and raw broker retained/pending/ack-pending/exhausted observations before, during, and after the API fault.
Fault injection timeline and terminal ledger demonstrating explicit unknown/unavailable status and later resolution of stranded work.
cases.acceptance: Status returns unresolved>=1 or an equivalent explicit exhausted-work state before resolution; API failure yields unknown, never healthy empty.
historical_evidence: Executed final-delivery probe showed stored=1 with pending=0 and ack_pending=0; source converts pending API errors to (0,0).

cases.title: Publish timeout has a single cancellation and reconciliation lifecycle
given: Reliable output channel is full; producer publish deadline P is shorter than the harness test deadline.

Each publish operation has a stable operation ID and outcomes accepted, definitely-rejected/cancelled, unknown, or unresolvable transport history; the reliable composition has durable intent or an idempotent recovery strategy.
fault_schedule: Begin publishing output A and block broker acceptance using a full channel.
Wait for caller deadline, then fail/retry the upstream computation.
Free broker capacity after the caller has returned and observe the original asynchronous operation.
assertions: If cancellation is reported definite, the original operation cannot later publish A.
If acceptance is ambiguous, the original send remains Unknown/Unresolvable when its history cannot be proven; the runtime preserves durable intent and must not assume nonpublication.

The composition recovers the logical output through durable intent and/or idempotent retry; duplicate transport deliveries may occur, but retry cannot create contradictory authoritative logical outcomes.
evidence: Operation-ID trace spanning durable publication intent, broker send/receipt events, caller timeout/cancellation result, and late broker acceptance observations.
Recovery/idempotent-retry ledger linking the unknown original send to its eventual logical output outcome without claiming unobservable transport history was resolved.
cases.acceptance: For each operation, reported acceptance/cancellation is truthful; no late publish follows a definitely-cancelled result. After broker recovery the reliable composition recovers an accounted logical output within R using durable intent/idempotent retry, while the original send may correctly remain Unknown/Unresolvable if native acceptance history is unavailable.
historical_evidence: Source audit: future.result(timeout=120) does not cancel the background retry coroutine.

cases.title: Lost publication acknowledgment preserves truthful deduplication guarantees
given: Broker has a finite native deduplication window W; durable workflow identity is separate from transport sequence.
fault_schedule: Allow broker to store A, then drop its acknowledgment before producer observes it.
Retry A with the same operation ID within W, then repeat recovery after advancing beyond W.
Compare raw deliveries, publish receipts, and logical completion outcomes.
assertions: Adapter never reports a lost PubAck as definite rejection.
Within a claimed idempotent-publish window the broker/adapter coalesces repeats as advertised.
Beyond that window the backend either has persistent operation reconciliation or explicitly permits duplicate delivery; runtime idempotency handles logical effects.
evidence: Broker deduplication configuration/window, dropped-PubAck fault trace, and retry timestamps on both sides of the window.
Raw publish/delivery receipts and logical completion ledger by stable operation ID, including duplicate deliveries and any unknown original-send status.
cases.acceptance: No accepted ID is lost. Observed duplicate behavior matches the declared window and capability contract; a backend claiming unlimited idempotent publish fails if it only relies on W.
historical_evidence: Source audit: fixed 120-second duplicate window and stable publish header do not establish unlimited exactly-once behavior.

cases.title: Live publication failures are observable and do not masquerade as acceptance
given: Disposable frame publisher supports nonblocking operation and exposes accepted, dropped, or unknown outcomes.
fault_schedule: Disconnect broker or force a real publish failure while sending 20 identified frames.
Reconnect and send a sentinel; separately simulate a lost publication acknowledgment.
Inspect metrics and receipt histories.
assertions: Failure/drop is visible with reason and count; a swallowed exception is not a confirmed acceptance.
Ambiguous acknowledgment loss is distinguishable from a deliberate drop.
Recovery preserves freshness and does not replay an unbounded stale client buffer.
evidence: Per-attempt live publication receipts with accepted/dropped/unknown classification and broker connection fault timeline.
Drop/queue-age metrics and post-reconnect sentinel delivery latency demonstrating bounded fresh recovery.
cases.acceptance: All 20 attempts reconcile to observed receipt states; no false confirmed-accepted receipt. Sentinel is delivered within the configured live recovery bound after reconnection.
historical_evidence: Source audit: REALTIME _do_publish returns success from every caught publication exception.

cases.title: Backpressure enforces both envelope count and payload-byte budgets
given: Reliable profile has small count and byte budgets; live profile has explicit overwrite/drop policy.
Inputs alternate 1KB and 1MB payloads, with readers intentionally paused.
fault_schedule: Publish until the earliest configured limit is reached.
Continue publishing under reliable and live profiles separately.
Resume readers and inspect queue, payload allocation, and publication receipts.
assertions: Reliable publication blocks or returns a typed capacity outcome without silently evicting accepted work.
Live applies the documented policy and reports drops.
Offloaded payload admission counts bytes held outside the broker; envelope max_msgs cannot conceal unbounded external images.
evidence: Timestamped message-count, payload-byte reservation, retained-object-byte, and in-flight-budget snapshots while readers are paused.
Per-ID publish receipts, reliable input checksums after drain, and live overwrite/drop records reconciling every capacity decision.
cases.acceptance: Observed retained payload bytes plus reserved admissions never exceed the declared budget by more than explicitly bounded in-flight reservations; accepted reliable inputs remain readable.
historical_evidence: Source audit: BATCH max_msgs=10000 bounds envelopes while Redis is 4GiB and can evict; 10000 offloaded 1MB frames exceed it.

cases.title: Shared consumer credit tracks useful concurrency without unbounded prefetch
given: Ten stateless worker replicas each hold at most one processing input and request a stage concurrency target of ten.
At least 20 inputs are available; a barrier prevents completion until all intended workers receive one.
fault_schedule: Start with target concurrency two and verify initial credit, then increase to ten.
Hold all processing at the barrier and measure distinct workers active versus messages merely prefetched.
Release work and scale down, observing total in-flight accounting.
assertions: Accepted concurrency-ten configuration can activate ten distinct workers without waiting for an earlier ACK; fixed consumer credit eight or six fails.
Extra credit remains bounded by processing plus explicitly configured prefetch, and is budgeted in bytes.
If the backend cannot resize credit safely, the scaling request is rejected with a capacity reason instead of adding idle replicas.
evidence: Effective consumer-credit configuration and ten-worker receive/processing-barrier timestamps before any completion is released.
Concurrency resize trace and in-flight/prefetch count/byte high-water measurements during scale-up and scale-down.
cases.acceptance: Ten workers reach the processing barrier before any completes when target ten is accepted; in-flight and prefetched inputs remain within declared bounds.
historical_evidence: Prior live GPU/distribution review probe: ten subscribers received only eight held deliveries because one shared consumer had MaxAckPending=8.

cases.title: Control retention is independent of frame eviction and full data queues
given: A frame channel has capacity one or is full; durable control is authoritative versioned run/epoch state with required terminal/final-sequence/abort evidence.
Control reader/controller can start late; append-only command history is required only if explicitly requested as a separate capability.
fault_schedule: Publish last data A, then completion state C with its epoch/version/final sequence, then delayed data B under the runtime protocol fixture.
Separately fill reliable data capacity and commit ABORT state for the same epoch with a newer authoritative version.
Retry stale completion C after ABORT, start the control reader late, and reconcile authoritative control state while frame traffic continues.
assertions: Data eviction cannot erase authoritative terminal/control state or evidence required to reconcile it; control updates cannot consume the only retained data slot.

A late reader reconstructs the authoritative epoch state, final sequence where applicable, and abort evidence through the declared control retention horizon. Safe state compaction is allowed; retaining every intermediate command is unnecessary unless requested.

Same-epoch stale completion cannot erase or reverse an accepted authoritative abort. Control remains independently observable while data publication is blocked; runtime tests separately establish whether a completion claim is valid.
evidence: Data publication/retention trace and versioned authoritative control snapshots with epoch, final-sequence, abort evidence, and any compaction events through capacity pressure.
Late-reader reconciliation result and stale-C retry decision proving same-epoch ABORT remains authoritative; effective data/control retention and capacity configuration.
cases.acceptance: Throughout the declared control horizon, late readers recover the authoritative epoch state and required terminal/final-sequence/abort evidence independently of data pressure. Same-epoch stale completion cannot erase an accepted abort. Compaction passes if these semantics survive; full command history is tested only when explicitly requested.
historical_evidence: Executed probe: EOS sharing max_msgs=1 evicted the final data frame; control/EOS share node stream.

cases.title: Broker identities are collision resistant across normalized names
given: Names include a.b versus a_b, Unicode/punctuation variants, and tuples whose hyphen-joined stream names collide.
A deterministic identity codec is part of the namespace abstraction.
fault_schedule: Generate subjects, streams, subscriptions, and DLQ identities for every tuple.
Provision two formerly colliding graphs concurrently and publish uniquely tagged sentinels.
Read each logical subscription and list ownership metadata.
assertions: Distinct accepted identities map to distinct physical resources, or the compiler rejects the collision before provisioning.
Subscription filters cannot cross run/flow/node boundaries.
Encoded identities are reversible or tied to exact owner metadata; truncation/hashing does not silently change ownership.
evidence: Generated namespace corpus and logical-to-physical identity mapping with explicit collision rejections where applicable.
Concurrent resource ownership inventory and paired sentinel subscription records proving flow/run/node isolation.
cases.acceptance: Property-generated distinct namespace tuples never silently share a physical identity; paired sentinels are visible only to their intended subscriptions.
historical_evidence: Source audit: sanitize is noninjective and delimiter-only stream names are ambiguous.

cases.title: Run teardown uses exact ownership and preserves other runs and DLQ
given: Same flow has runs r and r-x plus a flow-level DLQ; unrelated resources deliberately share a textual prefix.
fault_schedule: Provision both runs and store one sentinel in each plus a DLQ record.
Delete r while r-x publishes; inject one delete failure and retry cleanup.
Inspect resource ownership and all remaining sentinels.
assertions: Only resources whose exact owner is run r are deleted.
Flow-level DLQ and run r-x remain intact.
Incomplete cleanup is reported and retryable; listing failure is not represented as successful complete cleanup.
evidence: Exact ownership inventories before and after teardown, delete API call trace, and injected list/delete failure records.
Read-back sentinels for r-x and the flow DLQ plus cleanup result states showing incomplete cleanup until retry succeeds.
cases.acceptance: After successful cleanup only r resources are absent; r-x sentinel and DLQ evidence remain readable. A fault produces an incomplete-cleanup result until reconciled.
historical_evidence: Source audit: delete_run_streams uses startswith(vf-flow-run-) and suppresses list/delete errors.

cases.title: Durability profile validates replicas and storage rather than durable names
given: Deployment contract explicitly declares its tolerated failures, replica count, persistent storage, RPO/RTO, and payload durability.
Fixtures include default single broker with emptyDir, three brokers but stream replicas one, and three replicas with persistent storage.
fault_schedule: Compile and provision each fixture against a profile requiring tolerance of one broker/pod loss.
Inspect actual streams and mounted volume type, not only desired Kubernetes manifests.
Remove access to topology/configuration inspection in a separate parameterization.
assertions: emptyDir plus single replica cannot certify persistent recovery under pod/node loss.
Three broker pods do not substitute for stream-level replica count three.
Unknown storage/replication settings cannot silently satisfy a requested durability profile.
evidence: Requested durability/failure profile, rendered resources, and actual mounted-volume plus stream/consumer replica configuration snapshots.
Certification/validation decisions for every fixture, including explicit rejection or unknown status when effective configuration is unsuitable or unavailable.
cases.acceptance: Only fixtures whose effective broker and payload guarantees match the requested failure model certify; unsuitable fixtures are explicit expected-rejection tests.
historical_evidence: Source audit: stream config omits num_replicas; development broker is single replica with emptyDir.

cases.title: Accepted reliable work survives declared broker and pod failures
given: Certified replicated persistent deployment from MSG-021; 100 accepted records include in-flight and undispatched inputs.
Failure fixture declares exactly which failures are tolerated and provides a recovery bound R.
fault_schedule: Publish records and record successful receipts.
Kill the current stream leader, then in a separate clean fixture delete/recreate its pod while preserving supported storage.
Resume workers and compare retained records and terminal outcomes.
assertions: Within the supported fault model, accepted unresolved records and controls survive and eventually become readable.
No adapter overclaims power-loss/whole-cluster durability based only on background file writes; those require a distinct certified fixture.
Replicas converge and no data are fabricated from unavailable management counters.
evidence: Pre-fault successful publication receipts and accepted-ID ledger, cluster/volume configuration, and exact leader/pod failure timeline.
Fresh-worker payload/delivery/terminal-outcome reconciliation and measured recovery time for every fault in the claimed durability profile.
cases.acceptance: Every pre-fault accepted ID is completed or durably terminal after recovery within R, with zero unexplained loss for faults included in the certified profile.
historical_evidence: Required production validation not executed in prior single-server audit; omitted stream replication and ephemeral default storage are known gaps.

cases.title: Loss of quorum or storage capacity does not produce false durable receipts
given: Replicated deployment with independently faultable quorum links and a dedicated test volume with controlled free space.
fault_schedule: Remove quorum, attempt publication, and then restore it.
In a fresh fixture exhaust broker storage while attempting publication, then restore free space.

For timeout cases preserve the unknown original-send status and recover the logical output after restoration through durable intent and/or idempotent retry; inspect native acceptance history only where the backend can establish it.
assertions: No durable-success receipt is returned without the contractually required acceptance condition.
Requests end as typed unavailable/capacity/unknown outcomes within their deadlines rather than silently dropping or hanging forever.

Previously accepted work remains recoverable. The composition restores an accounted logical outcome without falsely claiming an old ambiguous send was accepted or rejected when that transport history is unobservable.
evidence: Quorum/storage exhaustion fault trace and per-operation send, receipt, deadline, accepted/rejected/unknown classification history.
Durable-intent/idempotent-retry and recovered logical-outcome ledger, retaining Unknown/Unresolvable for original send histories that cannot be established.
Post-recovery read-back of previously confirmed accepted records and effective durability configuration.
cases.acceptance: Each attempt reports a truthful outcome within P. Within R after restoration, the reliable composition recovers an accounted logical result; an old send may remain Unknown/Unresolvable. No confirmed durable accepted record is lost within the declared fault model, and no unknown send is relabeled definitely rejected without evidence.
historical_evidence: New production fault test derived from implicit durability configuration and ambiguous publish lifecycle; not previously executed.

cases.title: Replay history remains available after all working subscriptions complete
given: Working channel uses interest/work retention; archive profile requests a separate retention horizon H.
Publish an input with model/config/source provenance and archive pin.
fault_schedule: Complete and settle all working subscriptions.
Delete the originating run resources.
Request replay at H minus one test-clock tick, then after deliberate archive expiry.
assertions: Working ACKs and run teardown cannot erase archive history before H.
Replay reconstructs original identity/provenance without confusing replay attempt identity with original ingestion.
After expiry the API reports intentionally expired history, not a successful replay with missing inputs.
evidence: Original envelope/provenance identity and archive retention/pin records before working acknowledgments and run deletion.
Pre-expiry replay envelope/payload checksum and explicit post-expiry API result with controlled-clock timestamps.
cases.acceptance: Pre-expiry replay resolves the original envelope and payload after working ACKs and teardown; post-expiry request returns an explicit expiry outcome.
historical_evidence: Source audit: Interest retention is a processing buffer, not an independent archive; flow DLQ is retained but blobs are not pinned.

cases.title: Core NATS connection readiness and slow-consumer loss are explicit
given: Core-only live adapter declares no offline replay and has bounded client queues; connection and subscription readiness are distinct from construction.
fault_schedule: Publish before subscriber readiness, then after its ready barrier.
Pause reads until the configured slow-consumer policy activates, disconnect, and reconnect.
Send a fresh sentinel and inspect events and local queue age.
assertions: The adapter does not promise delivery of pre-subscription inputs or offline recovery.
Slow-consumer drops/disconnects are reported, stale queued frames are expired, and queues stay bounded.
Ready-barrier semantics are documented and the post-recovery sentinel reaches the subscriber within the live bound.
evidence: Core subscription-ready, connection/disconnection, and publication timestamp trace identifying pre-ready and offline attempts.
Bounded client queue/age metrics, slow-consumer loss events, and fresh sentinel delivery timing after reconnection.
cases.acceptance: No false durability claims; all observed losses belong to permitted live-loss conditions, bounded queues hold, and fresh delivery resumes after reconnect.
historical_evidence: New Core adapter conformance test; current implementation uses JetStream and no Core backend exists.

cases.title: Stream and subscription growth is measured against the supported graph limit
given: Adapter declares a maximum supported graph size and provisioning/recovery SLO; benchmark fixture records broker CPU/RAM/disk and stream/consumer counts.
Graph series varies nodes, edges, replicas, and concurrent runs independently.
fault_schedule: Provision graphs up to the declared limit, publish fixed compact messages, and restart the broker or controller.
Repeat complete run creation/teardown enough times to expose orphan EOS/process-specific consumers.
Attempt a graph beyond the advertised limit.
assertions: Resource growth matches declared topology complexity and teardown returns to a bounded baseline.
Provisioning, reconnect, and steady-state SLOs hold on the named hardware/configuration.
Over-limit graphs receive an explicit capacity rejection instead of partially provisioning an apparently healthy run.
evidence: Benchmark environment manifest, graph-size series, effective stream/consumer counts, and provision/recovery/steady-state latency results.
Broker resource time series across repeated create/teardown cycles and explicit over-limit validation/provisioning outcome.
cases.acceptance: Publish measured limits with hardware and versions; pass only when the declared SLO and bounded post-teardown resource baseline hold. No universal camera-count claim from this test.
historical_evidence: Source audit: per-node streams, per-edge/per-partition durables and per-process EOS consumers scale with graph and replica counts; not throughput-benchmarked.

cases.title: One-megabyte frames offload safely and enforce envelope limits
given: Fixture has a 1000x1000 uint8 frame exactly 1000000 bytes and inline threshold 512KiB.
Payload store records stored bytes; broker fixture exposes its maximum envelope size.
fault_schedule: Encode/publish the frame with a store, then retrieve and compare bytes.
Repeat without a configured store and with a threshold larger than the broker maximum.
Include threshold-minus-one and threshold-plus-one boundary specimens using serializer size rather than only ndarray.nbytes.
assertions: Large frame is represented by a compact reference and round-trips exactly.
Missing store and oversize envelope are typed admission/configuration failures before a false successful publication.
Offload threshold includes serialized payload/envelope overhead; setting an unsafe threshold cannot bypass the broker limit.
evidence: Fixture ndarray dimensions/type, exact original/stored/envelope byte lengths, round-trip checksums, and negotiated broker size limits.
Boundary-case publication results and side-effect trace for absent store and unsafe inline-threshold configurations.
cases.acceptance: Payload bytes match exactly; transmitted envelope fits negotiated broker limits. Absent store produces explicit failure and zero falsely accepted publications.
historical_evidence: Prior serialization measurement: 1000000-byte ndarray stored as 1000017 bytes and 210-byte sample envelope; defaults offload above 512KiB.

cases.title: Transient payload access failures retry without terminal loss
given: Accepted input A contains a valid external reference; underlying object exists and is immutable.
Fault injection targets payload GET independently of broker I/O.
fault_schedule: Raise ConnectionError, timeout, or temporary unavailable during first GET in separate cases.
Allow broker/runtime replacement or retry, then restore payload access.
Follow A with a valid inline sentinel to detect a stuck retrieval path.
assertions: No transient GET fault produces TERM or terminal poison classification.
Input and object remain owned and recoverable until processing succeeds.
A and sentinel eventually complete; transient failure is visible in diagnostics.
evidence: Payload GET fault injection/recovery trace, object existence/checksum observations, and retry/settlement events for A.
Completion ledger and recovery elapsed times for A and sentinel proving no infrastructure-only terminal outcome.
cases.acceptance: A completes within R after payload-store recovery with byte-identical data; no terminal settlement occurs solely because of transient GET failure.
historical_evidence: Executed prior probe: ConnectionError caused actual messenger to TERM A without DLQ while blob still existed.

cases.title: Permanent missing or corrupt payloads are explicitly accounted
given: Accepted envelopes reference a missing object, a truncated object, or a checksum-mismatched object.
Contract distinguishes disposable-loss handling from reliable terminal data-loss handling.
fault_schedule: Delete or corrupt the backing object before a consumer loads it.
Trigger retrieval and bounded retries according to classification.
Inspect terminal outcome, provenance, and continued processing of another input.
assertions: Reliable failure becomes an explicit durable data-loss/poison outcome rather than silent TERM or endless retry.
Live loss records an allowed missing/expired-payload drop with identity and reason.
Corruption cannot be passed silently to a model as valid original frame data.
evidence: Original reference/checksum, deliberate delete/corrupt operations, observed retrieval error classifications, and bounded retry history.
Per-input durable reliable terminal records or live drop events plus sentinel completion evidence.
cases.acceptance: Each broken reference has the correct observable terminal/drop outcome within its configured handling deadline; none is recorded as successful processing.
historical_evidence: Source audit: Redis missing object raises KeyError and all decode exceptions are terminally discarded without accounting.

cases.title: Lost broker ACK cannot reclaim payload needed for redelivery
given: One accepted frame has one logical reader and one outstanding payload ownership record.
fault_schedule: Process first delivery successfully.
Allow ordinary client ACK send to return but drop the ACK before broker acceptance or confirmation.
Observe release behavior, restart the worker, and cause redelivery.
assertions: A client-side send result cannot be mistaken for confirmed durable settlement.
Until settlement/reconciliation proves the reader is finished, either the payload or an equivalent durable recoverable copy remains accessible.
Redelivery can resolve original bytes and settle safely.
evidence: ACK send, dropped delivery/confirmation, broker settlement-status, and payload ownership/release event timeline.
Redelivery checksum and replacement completion record demonstrating bytes remained available throughout acknowledgment uncertainty.
cases.acceptance: No redeliverable accepted envelope points to unavailable bytes; replacement completes successfully and reclamation occurs only after the certified release condition.
historical_evidence: Source audit: handle ack() calls plain msg.ack() and then immediately releases the external blob.

cases.title: Release is idempotent by logical reader rather than delivery handle
given: Payload has two logical readers X and Y; X receives two delivery handles for the same message while Y is still outstanding.
fault_schedule: Complete X via its newer delivery and persist release.
Replay X release through the older handle, retry after a lost release response, and restart X.
Load the object from Y, then complete Y.
assertions: X reduces ownership exactly once across handles and processes.
Object remains available until Y and all other pins complete.
Repeated release after final cleanup is harmless and cannot affect a reused/different object.
evidence: Logical-reader/message/generation identities and every release request/response including duplicates, lost responses, and restart.
Ownership snapshots proving X decremented once, Y checksum before completion, and final GC timestamp after Y releases.
cases.acceptance: Ownership count after any number of X releases remains one; Y reads original bytes; after Y completes the object is reclaimed within the declared GC bound G.
historical_evidence: Source audit: _resolved is per Python handle, while Redis release blindly decrements one global counter.

cases.title: Crash after confirmed settlement does not leak a payload forever
given: Logical reader completion and payload ownership are durable or reconcilable; GC bound G is declared.
fault_schedule: Confirm broker input settlement.
Kill the worker before its payload release call.
Restart without the original in-memory handle and run reconciliation/GC.
assertions: The object remains safe during uncertainty but does not require the dead process to reclaim it.
Reconciliation releases the completed logical reader once using durable evidence.
Other outstanding readers and archive pins are preserved.
evidence: Confirmed settlement evidence, exact worker kill-before-release barrier, and ownership state persisted across restart.
Reconciliation decisions and GC/object-existence timeline for completed versus still-owned readers.
cases.acceptance: Final-reader objects are reclaimed within G after recovery; objects still owned by another reader remain readable throughout.
historical_evidence: Source audit: ACK and release are separate operations with no durable release reconciliation record.

cases.title: Creation crashes and partial publication produce bounded orphan recovery
given: Payload publication protocol exposes reservation, object creation, reader ownership creation, and envelope acceptance barriers.
fault_schedule: Crash in separate runs after object write but before ownership creation, after ownership creation but before envelope publish, and after accepted envelope but before publication receipt.
Restart the publisher and invoke reconciliation; repeat under lost object-store write response.
assertions: A partially created object is never exposed as a successfully accepted input before it can be resolved.
Unreferenced objects are eventually reclaimed without deleting an object referenced by an ambiguously accepted publication.
Duplicate retries use operation identity or reconcile all created objects.
evidence: Per-operation reservation/object/ownership/envelope acceptance journal and recorded crash point for each tested creation/publication boundary.
Post-recovery object-to-envelope reachability inventory, accepted-reference checksums, and orphan GC completion timestamps.
cases.acceptance: After recovery every accepted envelope resolves; every object lacking a live/replay/terminal reference is reclaimed within G. No counterless object persists beyond its bounded orphan policy.
historical_evidence: Source audit: Redis writes payload then separate counter, and messenger serializes/offloads before publish.

cases.title: Release remains atomic when ownership metadata expires or is evicted
given: Object is still legitimately owned by Y; X attempts release while metadata can disappear between operations.
A clustered-store fixture verifies key placement where atomic multi-key operations are used.
fault_schedule: Pause X after the equivalent of EXISTS(refcount) but before decrement.
Expire/evict or replace the counter, then resume X.
Run two final-reader releases concurrently, including lost responses and retries.
assertions: Release cannot recreate a negative counter and delete an object still needed by Y.
Generation/object identity fences stale operations against newly created ownership metadata.
Implementation is atomic in the actual supported store topology, including cluster key-slot constraints.
evidence: Controlled release interleaving trace including metadata expiry/replacement, generation identity, key-slot layout, and lost-response retries.
Ownership/object-state snapshots and Y read checksum proving no premature deletion, negative counter, or cross-generation mutation.
cases.acceptance: All enumerated interleavings preserve live references; no negative ownership record or cross-generation delete occurs. Final cleanup is idempotent.
historical_evidence: Source audit: Redis EXISTS then DECR then separate UNLINKs permits races; payload and counter keys use different cluster slots.

cases.title: Payload retention covers the entire accepted retry and outage horizon
given: Declared reliable recovery horizon H exceeds a short test TTL; accepted input remains outstanding at TTL.
Live fixture explicitly allows expiration and provides age/drop accounting.
fault_schedule: Stop the required reader, advance clock past TTL, and restart it before H.
Repeat while a lease renewal is delayed or the payload service is unavailable.
For live fixture allow expiry and inspect the resulting input disposition.
assertions: Reliable payload remains recoverable until completion, explicit terminal transfer, or an intentionally declared expiration outcome.
A TTL shorter than the promised recovery horizon is rejected or supplemented by a durable copy/pin protocol.
Live expiry is observable and does not masquerade as reliable recovery.
evidence: Retention/recovery contract, TTL/pin/renewal configuration, controlled clock schedule, and reader outage timeline.
Post-TTL protected-reference checksums or explicit prepublication configuration rejection; live-expiry drop records for disposable cases.
cases.acceptance: Every accepted reliable input still within H loads original bytes after the pause; incompatible retention configuration is rejected before publication.
historical_evidence: Source audit: fixed 3600-second REALTIME and 86400-second BATCH TTL are independent of outstanding work and retry lifetime.

cases.title: Evictable cache cannot certify durable payload storage
given: Store fixture includes Redis with volatile-lru and persistence disabled, and a candidate durable implementation.
Small memory cap allows deterministic pressure without large allocations.
fault_schedule: Keep a reliable frame outstanding while writing unrelated objects until cache eviction occurs.
Run live and reliable profile validation against each store.
Read the outstanding frame and inspect loss accounting.
assertions: An evictable store alone cannot certify reliable retention if needed objects can be evicted.
A durable tier or admission policy protects reliable bytes; merely tracking an envelope is insufficient.
Live cache eviction is allowed only with explicit identity/reason and bounded behavior.
evidence: Effective store eviction/persistence settings and contract-validation result for each cache-only or protected durable-tier fixture.
Memory-pressure/eviction timeline with protected-reference checksums or declared live missing-payload drop outcomes.
cases.acceptance: Reliable configuration either rejects the cache or demonstrates byte-identical recovery from a certified protected copy; live missing frames produce observable allowed-loss outcomes.
historical_evidence: Source audit: shipped Redis has maxmemory 4gb, volatile-lru, and disabled persistence.

cases.title: Payload-store restart obeys the declared persistence failure model
given: Accepted envelope outlives its publisher; all active workers are stopped to prevent in-memory copies masking loss.
Store deployment declares supported process/pod/node failure behavior.
fault_schedule: Write and accept frames, then restart the payload service process.
In separate certified fixtures delete/recreate its pod or remove one storage replica according to the declared fault model.
Start a fresh worker or replay reader.
assertions: All accepted protected references remain resolvable under claimed failures.
Broker survival does not substitute for independent payload durability.
Unsupported failure modes are explicitly excluded/rejected instead of being counted as passed durable recovery tests.
evidence: Accepted envelope/reference/checksum ledger and effective store persistence/replication/failure-profile configuration.
Process/pod/storage-replica failure trace and fresh-worker reads after recovery with proof original workers were stopped.
cases.acceptance: Fresh process reads byte-identical frames for every protected reference after each claimed supported fault; no recovery from a hidden worker cache is accepted.
historical_evidence: Source audit: nonpersistent Redis can lose all images while durable envelopes remain. No prior live Redis restart test.

cases.title: Dropped and disconnected-reader frames have a bounded reclamation path
given: Test workload writes 1MB frames with latest buffer one, two logical readers, and an explicit live ownership/drop horizon.
One reader is slow or disconnects permanently; clock and storage byte metrics are available.
fault_schedule: Publish at least 1000 frames while the slow reader never settles overwritten inputs.
Continue publishing beyond multiple reclamation horizons, then stop all publication.
Reconnect the reader or explicitly retire it and run GC.
assertions: Overwritten messages release/cancel their no-longer-required reader ownership through a durable or reconcilable path.
Memory plateaus at the declared live budget rather than growing at input_rate times the one-hour TTL.
A frame still legitimately in use is protected until its documented lease expires or reader is fenced.
evidence: Frame publication/drop/reader-disconnect timeline and per-reference ownership cancellation or reconciliation records.
Stored-byte/queue-byte time series over multiple reclamation horizons and final GC inventory after publication stops.
cases.acceptance: After steady state stored bytes remain within budget plus bounded in-flight allowance; after stop, all unpinned objects are reclaimed within G without deleting valid in-use frames.
historical_evidence: Source audit: broker max_msgs eviction has no external-blob release hook; missing one counted reader leaves object until TTL/eviction.

cases.title: Rejected and deduplicated publications do not accumulate unreachable blobs
given: Large-payload publisher creates a reference before attempting envelope publication; broker can reject or deduplicate by stable message ID.
fault_schedule: Force a full-stream rejection, a definite connection rejection, and a duplicate publication acknowledgment in separate runs.
Retry the same logical output ten times with identical bytes.
Inspect all created object IDs and reachability after reconciliation.
assertions: Any new object not referenced by the broker-accepted envelope is reclaimed.
Deduplication acknowledgment does not transfer ownership to a fresh blob that the retained original envelope never names.
Lost acceptance response is reconciled before reclaiming a possibly referenced object.
evidence: Publication operation-ID and created-object-ID trace for definite rejection, deduplication, and ambiguous receipt cases.
Broker-retained-envelope reference inventory, referenced-object checksums, and unreachable-object GC timestamps.
cases.acceptance: After G there is no unreachable object from definite rejection/deduplication; each actually retained envelope still resolves its exact referenced object.
historical_evidence: Source audit: each _publish re-encodes into a fresh UUID blob before applying broker Nats-Msg-Id deduplication.

cases.title: Dead letters retain images for the complete forensic and replay horizon
given: A frame-bearing input fails permanently; DLQ retention H is longer than ordinary payload TTL.
DLQ reader is offline until near H.
fault_schedule: Publish and confirm dead-letter outcome including payload retention ownership.
Advance past ordinary TTL, complete all normal readers, and delete the original run.
Read and replay the DLQ entry at H minus one tick.
assertions: The dead letter has an independent payload pin or durable copy lasting at least H.
Normal release and run teardown cannot delete forensic evidence.
An incomplete DLQ pin transaction cannot terminally release the source input; MSG-009 covers outage recovery.
evidence: DLQ acceptance, independent payload pin/copy confirmation, ordinary-reader completion, and run teardown event trace.
Near-horizon DLQ/replay frame checksum and provenance read-back plus intentional expiry record after H.
cases.acceptance: Original frame bytes and provenance are readable throughout H after normal input cleanup; expiry is deliberate and observable after H.
historical_evidence: Source audit: DLQ retains original raw envelope for seven days but does not pin its 1h/24h external blob.

cases.title: Large-payload DLQ routing inspects metadata without hydrating the image
given: DLQ includes one inline and one 1MB external-payload envelope naming the failed node and original parent.
Routing operation can parse envelope metadata independently of payload access.
fault_schedule: Run replay preview/routing with payload GET unavailable.
Restore payload access and execute replay through the supported replay path.
Compare selected target and replay success for inline and offloaded entries.
assertions: Determining producer/target identity does not require loading frame bytes.
Large valid entries are not silently skipped because decode_envelope lacks a BlobStore argument.
Actual replay verifies payload availability separately and reports a typed error if it cannot obtain the protected bytes.
evidence: Inline/offloaded envelope metadata parse and replay-preview routing output while payload GET is unavailable.
Instrumented GET log proving routing avoided hydration and post-restoration replay results or explicit payload access errors.
cases.acceptance: Inline and offloaded valid entries both produce the correct routing plan while GET is unavailable; execution succeeds for both after restoration or emits an explicit payload error.
historical_evidence: Source audit: CLI replay calls decode_envelope(data) without a blob store to discover producer_name, so blob envelopes are skipped.

cases.title: Replay has fresh ownership and intentional recipient scope
given: Original parent fed children X and Y; only X failed and has a dead letter.
Replay request explicitly targets X or explicitly requests whole-branch replay; original reader releases have already occurred.
fault_schedule: Replay the dead letter into the same run and a different run in separate fixtures.
Have Y complete a normal input concurrently and retry the replay publication acknowledgment.
Complete replayed work and inspect reader ownership and provenance.
assertions: Node-scoped replay does not unexpectedly reprocess Y by blindly publishing to the original parent broadcast subject.
Replay creates its own delivery/reader ownership without decrementing already-released original reader shares.
Target run identity, original lineage, and replay attempt identity remain distinct and consistent; retry does not create unowned payloads.
evidence: Replay request scope, original/replay/target-run identity mapping, and actual per-child delivery/completion ledger.
Original and replay ownership/pin snapshots through acknowledgment retry and checksum reads until all replay owners finish.
cases.acceptance: Observed recipient set equals the requested replay scope; replayed bytes remain readable until all replay owners finish, and original ownership cannot be decremented again.
historical_evidence: Source audit: CLI republishes original raw reference on parent subject with fresh header ID and no new payload reader ownership.

cases.title: Unchanged frames can traverse metadata stages without new image copies
given: Graph has five pass-through/metadata-only stages whose outputs refer to one unchanged immutable 1MB frame.
Payload store records PUT count, bytes written, unique object IDs, and reader/pin lifetime.
fault_schedule: Run 100 frames through all five stages and a slow final consumer.
Add metadata at each stage without mutating image bytes.
Complete all readers and inspect reclamation.
assertions: Reference-preserving publication uses one canonical image object per frame, or the backend explicitly declares/caps any necessary copy amplification.
Passing a reference preserves ownership for new downstream readers and cannot prematurely reclaim the image.
Actual image transformations create a distinct object while leaving earlier readers correct.
evidence: Per-frame/per-stage object-ID and metadata lineage trace plus payload PUT counts/bytes for unchanged versus transformed frames.
Stage checksum observations, slow-final-reader ownership timeline, and postcompletion GC inventory.
cases.acceptance: For the reference-forwarding capability, 100 unchanged frames create 100 canonical image objects rather than 500; every stage reads identical bytes and final cleanup completes within G.
historical_evidence: Source audit: every node publication serializes and stores a fresh UUID blob even for unchanged frames.

cases.title: Partition ownership is checked before loading large image bytes
given: Eight partitioned replicas receive routable metadata for 100 frames; each frame has exactly one assigned owner.
Payload GET is instrumented by replica and frame; completion routing is handled separately by runtime tests.
fault_schedule: Publish frames with keys spanning all partitions.
Block GET for one nonowner replica and verify its inability to fetch does not delay owners.
Count GET operations and bytes by ownership, including retries.
assertions: A nonowner does not fetch/decode the full frame merely to discard it.
Routing can use envelope metadata or broker partition subjects before hydration.
Legitimate retry fetches are separately attributed instead of hidden in nominal per-frame amplification.
evidence: Per-frame partition assignment and per-replica routing/GET log separating owner, nonowner, and retry fetches.
Aggregate useful-fetch byte count and owner progress trace during the blocked-nonowner GET fault.
cases.acceptance: For no-failure single-owner fixture, nonowner frame GET count is zero and useful frame fetch bytes are approximately N*S plus declared transport overhead, not replicas*N*S.
historical_evidence: Source audit: _pull_loop decode_envelope loads blob before _owns; prior sizing shows read traffic multiplying with partition replica count.

cases.title: Slow payload reads cannot block broker heartbeats or control delivery
given: Payload service can block GET for longer than broker ACK wait; another input is processing normally and a control subscriber shares the client runtime.
Adapter declares maximum concurrent payload requests and control latency L.
fault_schedule: Block one large GET on a real separate payload-service connection.
Send control/status requests and require keepalive for the unrelated active input.
Issue enough additional GETs to reach configured concurrency, then restore service.
assertions: Blocking payload I/O does not monopolize the broker event loop.
Keepalives/control operate within their deadlines while I/O workers/async requests remain bounded.
Restoration drains queued retrievals without exceeding payload memory/admission budgets.
evidence: Payload GET block/recovery timeline with active/queued I/O count and byte high-water measurements.
Concurrent broker keepalive/lease history and control/status latency samples proving deadlines hold during blocked payload I/O.
cases.acceptance: Control latency remains below L and unrelated inputs retain their valid leases; active GET count and queued bytes never exceed configured limits.
historical_evidence: Source audit: synchronous Redis GET runs inside asynchronous NATS pull loop during decode.

cases.title: Raw decoded frame size drives capacity estimates and admission
given: Fixtures include a compressed image near 1MB and its decoded 1920x1080x3 uint8 array of 6220800 bytes.
Capacity estimator receives actual serialized payload size and optional compressed-source metadata.
fault_schedule: Read/decode the source through the same reader/serializer path used by workers.
Attempt admission under a 2MB payload budget, then under an adequate budget.
Compare predicted stored bytes with instrumented payload writes.
assertions: Estimator cannot assume compressed input size equals interstage raw ndarray size.
Payload reservation accounts for serialized overhead and declared transient copies.
Unsafe admission is rejected/backpressured before writing an object larger than remaining budget.
evidence: Compressed-source size, decoded ndarray shape/dtype/nbytes, serialized object length, and capacity estimator/reservation output.
Admission decisions under 2MB and adequate budgets plus actual stored-byte measurements and declared transient-copy overhead.
cases.acceptance: 6220800-byte raw frame is never admitted against only 2MB available capacity; predicted stored-byte size agrees with measured serialized size, with separately declared allocator overhead.
historical_evidence: Prior measurement: decoded 1080p RGB frame is 6220800 bytes and stored payload 6220819 bytes; serializer writes contiguous raw ndarray bytes.

cases.title: Reader replacement and membership changes preserve logical ownership
given: Payload ownership belongs to logical subscriptions/partitions rather than ephemeral pod count.
A frame is outstanding during worker replacement and a permitted stateless scale event.
fault_schedule: Create a frame with original reader membership, then replace one worker and change replica count.
Redeliver to replacement while the original worker returns late and tries to release.
Retire a logical subscription using the explicit policy, then complete remaining readers.
assertions: Replacement of a worker does not add/delete a logical reader share accidentally.
Late fenced worker cannot release another generation owner or cause premature deletion.
Intentional subscription removal reconciles its pending ownership; a raw initial replica count cannot leak forever after scale-down.
evidence: Logical subscription/partition membership generations, worker replacement/scale/retirement trace, and stale-worker release attempts.
Ownership snapshots and required-reader checksums throughout transition, followed by final release-once and GC completion evidence.
cases.acceptance: Every still-required reader can resolve the frame throughout transition; final-reader count reaches zero exactly once after allowed retirement/completion and GC finishes within G.
historical_evidence: Source audit: compiler computes blob_readers from initial child/partition replica count; release has no logical-reader identity.

cases.title: Frame-path capacity benchmark measures useful throughput and total byte amplification
given: Named hardware/network/store versions and explicit workload parameters: cameras C, frame rate f, postdecode bytes S, frame-bearing stages K, consumers R, and hold time W.
Run includes one 1MB@30FPS baseline, fan-out, partition replication, and a slow consumer; this is a capacity experiment, not an assumed camera-count guarantee.
fault_schedule: Increase camera count until freshness or reliable latency SLO first fails.
Repeat for fan-out/partition counts 1,2,4,8 and image-bearing stage counts 1 and 5.
Pause one reader for W, resume, and measure both steady-state and peak memory, network ingress/egress, GET/PUT bytes, serialization CPU, and drops.
assertions: Measurements distinguish useful owner processing from replica fetch/discard and repeated unchanged-frame writes.
Read and write network directions are reported separately; hourly throughput volume is not labeled retained storage.
Memory agrees with retained-reference lifetime plus documented buffers/overhead; no unbounded orphan slope or hidden eviction sustains apparent throughput.
evidence: Reproducible hardware/software/network environment and workload manifest specifying C, f, S, K, R, W, SLOs, and headroom.
Throughput/frame-age/drop/latency and CPU/memory time series with directional network and payload GET/PUT byte amplification metrics.
Slow-reader pause/recovery measurements and final object reachability/eviction inventory separating sustainable useful throughput from leaked or discarded work.
cases.acceptance: Publish the maximum load meeting explicit SLOs with full environment and amplification factors; admission limit must be no greater than the measured sustainable capacity with declared headroom. Passing is workload-specific, not a universal scale claim.
historical_evidence: Prior analytical sizing identified CfS write traffic, CfSR read traffic, CfSW retained bytes, and extra repeated-stage/partition amplification; no hardware performance test was previously run.

cases.title: Reject layouts exceeding physical MIG memory
given: A checked-in independent hardware fixture describes one H100-80GB, seven compute slices and the documented memory-slice requirements; fixture provenance and device revision are recorded.

Direct geometry fixture requests four 1g.20gb profiles and three 1g.10gb profiles on one H100-80GB, independently of a workload usable-byte request. Also replay the source numeric 20-unit/10-unit demand as a separate historical variant; nominal profile labels are not exact usable GiB.
fault_schedule: Run planning without any cluster mutation capability.
Evaluate every returned plan with the independent fixture oracle, not the planner's fit() or its profile registry.
assertions: Planner rejects this one-card demand or produces a valid multi-card plan only when extra inventory is actually supplied.
No plan claims memory slices beyond the physical card; no GPU mutation is attempted for rejected demand.
The direct-profile fixture reaches aggregate-memory validation; rejecting one slice for a literal usable-byte mismatch cannot pass the geometry regression.
evidence: Input inventory, demand, planner result and independent constraint evaluation.
Mutation audit showing zero writes for the rejected plan.
adapter_requirements: Separately maintained vendor-derived profile fixture and mutation recorder.
cases.acceptance: The one-H100 regression is rejected; every accepted plan satisfies both independently counted memory and compute slice limits.

cases.title: Validate MIG placement constraints independently of slice totals
given: MIG hardware family and firmware/driver versions are identified.
Generate mixed-profile requests whose aggregate memory/compute fit but whose legal start positions differ; include valid boundary layouts.
fault_schedule: Compare planned placements against NVML GPU-instance profile placement queries or a pinned authoritative vendor placement table.
On an isolated drained GPU, create accepted placements through the tested allocation adapter; query actual GPU/compute instances independently.
assertions: Accepted layouts have legal nonoverlapping placement intervals and meet each requested profile.
Invalid layouts fail before destructive changes; valid layouts are not universally rejected as a shortcut.
Dynamic DRA assertions inspect actual allocated geometry rather than requiring Videoflow to retain a private solver.
evidence: Profile placement query output, instance start/size and UUID inventory before/after.
Rejection result and mutation timeline for invalid cases.
adapter_requirements: Drained hardware fixture and reset/restore facility; unsupported GPU families are explicitly not covered.
cases.acceptance: Every accepted sampled layout can be instantiated exactly; all independently known impossible layouts are rejected without changing the card.

cases.title: Do not accept stale MIG terminal status for a new operation
given: Real Kubernetes API stores geometry A with state=success and an operation requesting geometry B; repeat with old state=failed.
A controllable MIG reconciler separates desired-label persistence, controller observation, physical application and terminal status publication.
fault_schedule: Hold the reconciler after the new desired configuration is written; return a real API read containing B's desired label and A's old terminal status.
Run both prepare and restore; then publish the operation-correlated completion only after the independent geometry observer sees B.
assertions: Old success does not release the prepare/restore barrier; old failure does not terminate B as failed.
Restore records, ownership and needed ConfigMaps remain until B is physically ready.
Timeout produces an explicit incomplete operation with recovery state.
evidence: Resource-versioned watch trace and request/response timing.
Operation identifiers, geometry observation and state transition journal.
adapter_requirements: Real API event/reordering harness; do not merely stub a success-returning method.
Observable operation identity and separate physical-readiness predicate.
cases.acceptance: Neither lifecycle direction completes during the stale-status interval; completion occurs only for the requested geometry after independent readiness.
cases.qualification_notes: The primary fixture can establish API/lifecycle invariants. Any physical device preparation, restoration, visibility or topology assertion also requires a real-GPU variant; mocks do not qualify that claim.

cases.title: Enforce exclusive GPU ownership under simultaneous claim attempts
given: Two independent allocation-controller/deploy processes plan the same initially unowned GPU node.
Both can read and write the real node object.
fault_schedule: Barrier both clients after reading the same resourceVersion and before their ownership writes.
Release both writes concurrently; repeat with reversed response delivery and a controller restart after the winner commits.
Release/rollback the loser after a successor has validly acquired a different ownership epoch.
assertions: Exactly one ownership epoch wins; the other sees a real API conflict and never applies geometry.
A stale rollback cannot remove another owner's label or lease.
Ownership survives process restart through durable API state.
evidence: API audit including conflict status/resourceVersions and both process logs.
Geometry mutation journal grouped by owner/epoch.
adapter_requirements: Two-process controller harness with real API precondition conflicts.
Barrier at allocation write boundary; authoritative owner/epoch observer.
cases.acceptance: Across both deterministic interleavings exactly one owner can mutate the card and every stale release is rejected; checking command argv alone is insufficient.

cases.title: Keep another flow's MIG configuration during last-owner teardown
given: Flow A is the last recorded owner of a shared MIG configuration; flow B is able to allocate a different node.
Shared ConfigMap and ClusterPolicy are real API objects.
fault_schedule: Pause A after its last-owner read.
Allow B to acquire ownership and publish its configuration, then resume A's cleanup.
Repeat with A/B responses reordered, and with a crash between A's entry removal and global-pointer decision.
assertions: B's configuration entry and referenced ConfigMap survive.
Global policy remains pointed at a configuration containing every active owner's entries.
A can finish its own cleanup without revoking B's resources.
evidence: API resourceVersion/audit timeline.
Active owner set, policy pointer and ConfigMap contents after each barrier.
adapter_requirements: Serialized shared-state coordinator or equivalent atomic protocol exposed through the adapter.
Concurrent real API publishers and crash injection.
cases.acceptance: No reachable interleaving deletes or disconnects configuration required by a live owner; all A-only state is eventually reclaimable.

cases.title: Preserve recoverability when MIG restore or policy restoration fails
given: An active allocation has durable original geometry and policy-pointer records.
Failures can be applied separately to geometry restore, policy patch, operator rollout and ConfigMap deletion.
fault_schedule: Restore geometry successfully but make the API reject restoration of ClusterPolicy; also test temporary RBAC denial and transport timeout with an ambiguous write outcome.
Restart cleanup in a new process after restoring access.
Repeat a failure at each subsequent cleanup boundary.
assertions: Referenced configuration is never deleted after failed/unconfirmed policy restoration.
Necessary original-state records persist until independently verified restoration.
Retry discovers committed writes and completes idempotently without restoring the generated geometry as the original.
evidence: Fault schedule, API audit and persisted recovery records.
Independent before/after geometry and mounted-configuration observations.
adapter_requirements: API fault proxy plus operator rollout observer.
cases.acceptance: Every injected failure leaves either the original active allocation or a durable resumable restore; no live pointer references a deleted configuration.
cases.qualification_notes: The primary fixture can establish API/lifecycle invariants. Any physical device preparation, restoration, visibility or topology assertion also requires a real-GPU variant; mocks do not qualify that claim.

cases.title: Treat failed occupancy and ownership reads as unknown
given: A running foreign pod holds a GPU; node and pod API permissions can be controlled independently.
For cleanup, another flow owns geometry and its ConfigMap entry.
fault_schedule: Deny or time out pod-list reads while node inventory still succeeds; also return malformed/truncated responses through the transport fault proxy.
Separately fail node-list and ConfigMap reads during cleanup.
Restore API access and retry.
assertions: Unknown occupancy is not interpreted as zero in use; no repartitioning or successful safety admission occurs from this snapshot.
Unknown owners/configuration are not interpreted as last-owner/empty.
Diagnostic identifies the failed dependency and retry can recover.
evidence: Real API error/status traces and normalized inventory completeness flags.
Foreign workload/device continuity and zero unsafe mutation count.
adapter_requirements: Inventory result must distinguish empty, unavailable and partial.
RBAC/transport fault injection with a continuously observed foreign allocation.
cases.acceptance: All read failures block the unsafe decision before mutation; the foreign allocation remains intact and a later complete snapshot permits normal progress.

cases.title: Use identical eligibility scope for GPU classification and capacity
given: Eligible pool contains whole GPUs; a time-sliced or MIG node outside the pool advertises the same resource name.
Additional nodes are excluded by taints, selectors or explicit topology requirements.
fault_schedule: Submit a valid multi-GPU demand to the eligible pool.
Change only out-of-scope nodes' sharing labels and repeat.
Change a selected node's evidence and refresh the planning snapshot.
assertions: Out-of-scope labels do not change classification or feasibility.
Capacity, sharing semantics and per-pod fit use the same eligible-node snapshot.
